metadata.title: Cisco Grows Into Its Multiple, And The Market Has To Do The Rest

content.text:
Consensus has the earnings arriving, and the multiple falling, yet the scenario that follows leaves a holder within a few percent of today's price unless the market goes on paying a richer forward multiple than it does today.
Cisco Systems (CSCO) trades at about $111 a share, roughly 30 times the last twelve months of normalized earnings. That is a demanding price for a networking company; the defense is that the earnings analysts expect will grow into it. They would. What that is worth to a holder is the smaller answer.
Thirty Times Today, Twenty Times On Fiscal 2028 Earnings
Today's price is about 21.5 times the earnings analysts expect for fiscal 2027, and about 20.0 times what they expect for fiscal 2028, a multiple 34% lower than the trailing one. That drop is not an earnings growth rate: the trailing figure is normalized net income with stock-based compensation added back, a basis not defined identically to the analysts' own adjusted earnings, so the two multiples are not a like-for-like series. Consensus for fiscal 2027, about $5.13 a share on the analysts' adjusted basis, is barely ahead of the $5.05 to $5.11 non-GAAP range management guided.
Margins Have To Hold While The Mix Fights Them
Consensus assumes profit margins hold roughly steady across the two forward years, and the business is what makes that an assumption. What changes the mix is AI infrastructure for hyperscalers: under 2% of revenue in fiscal 2025, about 6% of fiscal 2026 revenue of $63.3 billion, and $7.5 billion management projects for fiscal 2027. That business ships high volumes of hardware, Silicon One-based systems and optics, and management expects a slight gross margin headwind through fiscal 2027.
What protects profitability is the expense line, not the gross margin: capturing that growth needs minimal additional spend, management says, and its guide implies a non-GAAP operating margin of about 35% for fiscal 2027, which management calls a company high watermark, up from the prior-year 34.8%. A profit line reaching a company high while the revenue mix works against it is the kind of quality the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for.
Not Overpaying Is Not A Gain
If the share price never moves, by fiscal 2028 the stock trades at about 20.0 times the expected earnings: not overpaying, which is not the same as a gain. Price gains need the market to pay more than that. Cash does come back meanwhile: $12.7 billion of buybacks and dividends in fiscal 2026, 99% of free cash flow. Settle at about 20.8 times fiscal 2028 earnings, between the two forward multiples, and the stock is worth about 4% above today's price. A gain beyond that requires the market to pay a richer forward multiple than either of today's - the real bet embedded in owning the stock from here. The earnings underlying that math are a range: thirteen analysts, $5.07 to $6.12 a share for fiscal 2028. In past market shocks the stock has fallen as much as 52% from peak to trough, and no consensus path prices that in.
